title: Make a Teacher, Acquire a Friend
hookLine: people choose a community by warmth, practice and place
carry: make a teacher, acquire a friend

cards: The real estate agent has shown the kitchen, the yard and the closets. Then the couple asks a question she didn't expect: how long is the walk to the synagogue?

They don't drive on Shabbat, so the shul they choose will help decide the street they live on, and the street will help decide the shul. Other families ask other first questions. Who will know our names?
Will the prayers sound like the ones we grew up with?

teach.h: WARMTH: A FACE BEFORE A PLATFORM.
teach.b: Where you belong. Four turns. First, warmth.
Ask people why they joined their synagogue, and the answer is sometimes a person. Someone greeted them by name the second time they came. Someone brought soup when the baby was born.
The rabbi remembered their father's name. People sometimes follow a face before they follow a platform. Second, practice.
A community has to fit the way you live. Hebrew or English, fast or slow? Do men and women sit together?
How is Shabbat kept, and how strictly is that expected of you?

teach.h: PRACTICE: A FIT FOR YOUR LIFE.
teach.b: A warm room that asks for a life you don't want, or makes no room for the life you do, can be hard to stay in. Third, place.
For Jews who don't drive on Shabbat, the synagogue has to be within walking distance, so where they live and where they pray decide each other. For others, place means a commute, a city, or a screen.

teach.h: MAKE A TEACHER, ACQUIRE A FRIEND.
teach.b: In the Mishnah, Joshua ben Perachiah says: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend. Make, and acquire: both are things you do. He doesn't say which teacher or which friend.
Some people find their place on the first try. Some change places as their lives change: a student group, a young family's synagogue, a quiet minyan in old age.
Some belong to two. The tradition doesn't push toward one right answer. It pushes toward a teacher and a friend somewhere, people you can call my people.

how: Jews choose a synagogue or community by its people, its practice and its location; those who walk on Shabbat live within walking distance of the synagogue they attend.

o: the synagogue your family joined when you were born
whichever community lives closest to your home
a community chosen for warmth, practice and place

games.q: where you belong — tap the pairs.
p: a fit for the way you live
make a teacher, acquire a friend

s: Joshua ben Perachiah says to wait for a teacher and a friend to find you
he says make for yourself a teacher and acquire for yourself a friend: both take effort.
for Jews who walk on Shabbat, place helps decide the synagogue

games.q: you've moved to a new city and tried two synagogues. one is beautiful, and nobody spoke to you. one is plainer, and someone asked your name. what does today's lesson weigh?
o: the more beautiful room, and nothing else.
warmth, practice and place, and a teacher and a friend.
nothing: stay home until a perfect fit appears.
games.why: warmth, practice and place all count, and Joshua ben Perachiah says make for yourself a teacher and acquire for yourself a friend.

practice: Name the people you would call my people: a synagogue, a church, a family, a team, a few friends, or nobody yet.
Take the three questions one at a time: who there knows your name, does it fit the way you live or ask you to hide part of it, and can you actually get there?
Don't decide anything; just notice where the answers are strong and where they are thin, and if you pray, bring that picture into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Where you belong. A community chosen by warmth, practice and place, where you can make a teacher and acquire a friend. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: make a teacher, acquire a friend. Both are things you do, and together they make a place yours. Back tomorrow, same hill.
